When used as an adjective, "bully" means excellent, first-rate, or very good. It is a word of strong, enthusiastic approval. When someone describes something as "bully," they are saying it is outstanding, admirable, or of high quality.

This meaning is completely unrelated to the more familiar meanings you probably already know — the noun "bully" (a person who intimidates or harms others) or the verb "to bully" (to intimidate someone). As an adjective, "bully" is entirely positive and has nothing to do with threats or cruelty. The two meanings just happen to share the same word.

"Bully" as an adjective is not a mild or lukewarm compliment. It carries a sense of delight and enthusiasm. When someone calls something "bully," they are not just saying it is "okay" or "decent" — they are expressing genuine, wholehearted admiration, almost like cheering. Think of it as the equivalent of saying "Brilliant!" or "Splendid!" — words that go beyond simply "good."

• "That's a bully idea!" → "That's an excellent idea!"
  • "He's a bully fellow." → "He's a fine, admirable man."
  • "We had a bully time at the fair." → "We had a wonderful time at the fair."
  • "What bully weather for a walk!" → "What magnificent weather for a walk!"

In each case, notice that "bully" appears before a noun and describes it positively, just like any adjective would.

You will often see "Bully!" used all by itself, as an exclamation. In this case, it means "Excellent!" or "How wonderful!" It is the equivalent of shouting "Bravo!" or "Splendid!" after hearing good news or seeing something impressive. The adjective has simply been shortened into a one-word cheer.

One phrase where you might still encounter this word today is "Bully for you!" In its original, sincere form, this phrase means "Good for you!" or "How wonderful for you!" — it was a cheerful expression of praise or congratulations.

However, in modern spoken English, "Bully for you!" is very often used sarcastically. When said with a flat or dismissive tone, it means roughly "So what? I couldn't care less" or "Well, aren't you special." This is a classic case of a compliment being flipped into an insult through tone. So when you encounter this phrase, context and tone will tell you which meaning is intended — genuine praise or sarcastic dismissal.
"Bully Pulpit" — A Phrase Still Alive Today

One very common modern phrase that preserves the adjective meaning of "bully" is "bully pulpit." This phrase was coined by U.S. President Theodore Roosevelt, who was well known for using "bully!" enthusiastically as his favourite expression of approval.

Roosevelt used the phrase to describe the presidency as a "bully" (excellent, wonderful) "pulpit" (a platform from which one speaks to an audience). A bully pulpit, therefore, means an excellent, prominent platform or position of authority that gives someone the power to speak to many people and influence public opinion. Today, this phrase is widely used in politics and journalism. For example, journalists might write that a world leader is "using the presidency as a bully pulpit to push for climate policy."

This phrase is proof that the adjective "bully" is not entirely dead — it lives on in this expression, even if most people using it today no longer think about what "bully" originally meant.
The Historical Period — When Was This Word Used?

This adjective form of "bully" was most common in 19th and early 20th century British and American English. It had the energy and informality of slang, but it was widely used across both spoken and written language of that era. Theodore Roosevelt (U.S. President from 1901 to 1909) was so famously associated with the word that his enthusiastic use of "Bully!" became a defining part of his public personality.

By the mid-20th century, this usage had faded significantly. In everyday modern English, almost no one uses "bully" as an adjective to mean "excellent." If someone did use it today in casual speech, it would sound deliberately old-fashioned, theatrical, or comical — like someone putting on a Victorian costume in words.
How to Spot It in Older Writing

When you read novels, plays, or documents from the 1800s or early 1900s, you may encounter sentences like:

  • "What a bully adventure!"
  • "Bully sport, wouldn't you say?"
  • "He was a bully sort of chap."

In all these cases, "bully" is functioning as an adjective meaning "excellent" or "first-rate." You can almost always tell it is being used in this positive sense because it appears right before a noun it is describing, and the context is clearly one of praise or admiration — not intimidation.

If you see "Bully!" as a one-word sentence or exclamation in older writing, it simply means "Excellent!" or "Wonderful!" — a cheer of approval.

The adjective "bully" means excellent, first-rate, very good. It is enthusiastic and warm, not just mildly positive. It was widely used in 19th and early 20th century English, particularly associated with the energy and spirit of that era. Today, it is archaic in everyday speech, but it survives in two notable places: the phrase "bully pulpit" (an excellent platform of influence) and the phrase "Bully for you!" (which can mean either sincere congratulations or sarcastic dismissal, depending on tone). It has nothing to do with the modern meaning of "bully" as an intimidating person — the two meanings simply share the same spelling and sound.
